To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

burnout sufferers in the Netherlands are often legitimated as hard working, committed and altruistic, and are often understood to need to work less hard, not to be so committed and altruistic and to have a better work-life balance.
burnout is a condition which is widely accepted and understood as a legitimate illness, despite its close association with ontological doubt and moral suspicion.
burnout is an illness category which, in the Netherlands, is relatively widely accepted and legitimized, despite the fact that it shares some features with conditions which are commonly stigmatized.
In summary, our research is concerned with

how burnout sufferers and professionals make sense of the condition in relation to their own and wider socio-cultural lifeworlds, and how this relates to the political economy of the employment system.

how burnout sufferers and professionals negotiate the condition in the context of a particular national healthcare system, and how this relates to the wider political economy and lifeworld of the Netherlands.
understanding burnout as a social condition, and the ways in which it is experienced, diagnosed and managed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
burnout is a legitimate illness category, which has been accepted and incorporated into Dutch lifeworlds and healthcare system, albeit with tensions and contradictions.

burnout is an illness which, in the context of the Dutch employment system, is often recognized and accepted, and is often treated in terms of its moral implications, but that this recognition and treatment is often contradictory and ambivalent.

the Dutch healthcare context is a relatively favourable one in which burnout sufferers are able to access care, and in which burnout care is relatively acceptable to both patients and healthcare providers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

burnout is not a simple, one-dimensional response to the pressures of modern working environments, but is instead the outcome of the complex interplay of individual, institutional and structural factors.
, despite the lack of stigma, the legitimation of burnout is problematic, and that the condition remains a contested category, which is not easily understood as a medical illness.

the legitimation and stigma associated with burnout are complex and contradictory, and that burnout sufferers' narratives of illness and care are best understood in light of the interplay between the lifeworld and political economy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
burnout, and other illnesses with a similar social and cultural profile, are not simply a reflection of the social world but also a part of the social world, which in turn shapes the social world.
burnout is not a straightforward reflection of working environments.
burnout is a condition that is both socially produced and socially reproduced, and that it is important to understand the social context in which burnout is experienced and diagnosed.
